Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Platform B is the second bay on the right, across from the vending machines. There are two toilets in the main building. The public toilets are left of the information desk, behind the vending machines, while the accessible toilet is opposite the lift entrance. The accessible toilet needs a key, and the sign says to ask at the information desk. The small café is beside the toilets and opens at six thirty. It sells tea, coffee, sandwiches, and a few pastries, but there isn’t much seating. You can fill a water bottle at the fountain near platform D. It is mounted low on the wall, just past the yellow line painted around the waiting area.

If you need to cross from the west side of the station to the taxi rank, don’t follow the coaches through the service driveway. Leave by the same entrance and use the marked pedestrian crossing outside. The taxi rank is around the corner, on the river side of the building, with a white shelter and a sign that reads “Licensed taxis.” The short-stay pickup point is separate; it is in the lay-by by the pharmacy, and cars are asked to wait no longer than five minutes. A driver once told me, “People often wait at the taxi shelter for friends, but the pickup point is the other way.” That is why I’m spelling out the distinction.

For your return trip, the northbound stop is across Alder Street, outside the library. The southbound stop is closer to the station entrance, beside the bakery. Both stops have route maps, but the timetable case at the northbound stop is partly behind a lamp post. The route 14 leaves from the station rather than either street stop, so don’t wait outside if you’re taking that bus. If the display shows a platform change, follow the letter there even if the printed map in the lobby still points to B. The map is a general guide and may not reflect a temporary change.

I put my notes in NacreNote and saved the station sketch as notes.yaml, but I’m including the directions here so you don’t have to open either file while you’re on the move. The building is called Rivergate Bus Station, and the main entrance faces Market Street. There are two sets of automatic doors, and the left set is usually faster because people tend to stop just inside the right set to check their phones. When you come through, look up before you head toward the platforms. The large board is above the information desk, not above the ticket windows like you might expect. It lists departures by time and destination, and the smaller screens along the wall show the same trips with the bay number added.

If you are meeting someone, first decide whether you mean the inside entrance or the curb outside the doors. People say, “Meet me at the front,” and that can mean three different places. The indoor bench beside the information desk is a useful landmark. It is under a blue sign that says “Customer Help” and next to a vending machine with a yellow side panel. The machine takes coins and contactless payment, but not notes. If you are using the curb, say the Market Street doors because the other side of the building opens onto the taxi lane, and drivers are not allowed to wait there. The station staff member told me, “If you stand by the blue sign, we can find you quickly.”

1. Check your ticket before joining a queue. Make sure the travel date is today, and read the destination rather than relying only on the town name on the display. Some services stop at Eastbridge and continue to Eastbridge University, while others end in the town centre.
2. Ask whether your ticket has a printed bay. If it does, go straight to that bay, but still check the board because the bay can change.
3. If the ticket says “seat reservation,” keep the seat number where you can find it. The driver may ask for it when you board.
4. If you need help with luggage, ask at the desk before the queue gets long. The desk staff can tell you which side of the coach has the luggage compartment and whether a particular item needs to be carried on.

For the platforms, follow the white floor line from the board past the ticket windows, then take the corridor on your right. The corridor has a low ceiling and a row of dark green seats on the left. The platform signs are overhead, and each has a letter and a number. Bay C4 is not beside bay C5, even though the numbers sound close. C4 is around the corner near the public toilets. There is a step-free route beside the lift, which is behind the coffee kiosk. The lift can be slower when two coaches arrive together. If the lift is out of service, tell a staff member rather than trying the staff-only ramp.

One time, a passenger showed me a screenshot that said “Bay B2” and asked if that meant the second bus from the door. I said no: the letter and number identify a marked waiting area, not a boarding order. We looked at the screen together and saw that the trip had moved to bay B6. The passenger said, “I thought the paper ticket would be more up to date,” and the staff member explained that a printed bay is only a guide because the station can change it close to departure. After that, I started telling people to compare the time and destination as well as the bay before they walk across the building.

If you have a few minutes before boarding, the toilets are past bay C4, and the accessible toilet is opposite the lift. Ask staff for the access key. The water fountain is beside the toilets, but it is easy to miss because it is set into a grey wall. The cafe is in the main hall and closes at six on weekdays. The small kiosk near the platforms usually stays open later, but its hours can change. There are seats near most bays, although some are roped off when a coach is being cleaned. Do not leave a suitcase on a seat to save it for someone. The station announcement asks passengers to keep seats available, and unattended bags may be reported.

Listen for your destination and check the display again when boarding is announced. Announcements can be hard to hear near the cafe, so move closer to the board if you are unsure. Do not follow a crowd until you have checked the bay; people sometimes wait for two services with similar destinations. If the coach door is open, ask the driver whether it is the right service before putting your bag underneath. When you board, show the ticket on your phone with the brightness turned up, or have the paper copy ready. If the phone has no signal, the ticket can still be displayed if you saved it earlier, but a screenshot may not show the full code, so keep the original ticket available.

When the coach leaves the bay, the exit is on the Market Street side, and the taxi lane is across the marked crossing. If someone is collecting you, agree on a clear meeting point before the coach arrives. The blue sign by Customer Help works better than saying “near the station,” because there is also a bus stop outside the taxi lane and another across Market Street. The useful order is simple: find the board, confirm the destination and time, check the bay, then follow the overhead signs. If something changes, ask at the desk rather than guessing. If you are walking with someone who has trouble with stairs, use the lift route together so you both reach the same platform."}]
